text: Discount authority. Sales staff and account managers may approve a discount of up to 5 percent on the quoted price. Any discount above 5 percent needs the approval of the sales director, whatever the order volume and however small the difference. A request for approval states the customer's target price, the annual volume and the conditions that have already been agreed.

Custom housing policy. Housings or connectors that differ from the standard versions are produced from a minimum quantity of 300 units per order. The minimum has no exceptions, and custom orders are not combined with other customers' orders to reach it. Tooling is charged once.

Lead times. Standard catalogue items ship within 4 weeks of order, configured variants within 6 to 8 weeks, custom variants within 12 weeks after drawing approval. The 50 fastest-moving items are held in regional stock. Confirmed delivery dates are binding once the order confirmation has been issued.

Warranty and support. The warranty period is 24 months from delivery. Application engineers support commissioning by telephone and video call; visits to a customer's plant are arranged through the regional sales manager. Replacement units for warranty cases ship from regional stock.

Payment and delivery terms. Standard payment term is 30 days net. New customers pay the first order in advance or against a letter of credit. Export deliveries are quoted FCA or CIF. Annual framework agreements fix price and call-off quantities for 12 months.

Customer audits. Customers may audit production, calibration handling and serial-number traceability at the company's premises. Audits are arranged through the quality department with two weeks' notice and take half a day to a full day. Calibration records are kept for ten years and can be shown for any serial number.

Reference material. The company keeps written application reports organised by application type, such as conveying, dosing, winding, cutting and washing. Each report names the customer only with that customer's consent. Reports are released by the regional sales manager.

Evaluation quantities. Orders below the usual annual quantity are accepted for standard catalogue items at list price conditions. They do not change the terms of an existing framework agreement. Custom variants are excluded because of their minimum quantity.

An opportunity is qualified when three things are known: the money that has been allocated, the person who signs the purchase, and the date by which the customer needs the goods. Interest from engineering shows a need. It does not show that an order can be placed.
source: Adapted from the MEDDIC qualification framework

text: In machine building the engineer who selects a component and the person who releases the purchase are usually different people. An engineer's statement about urgency or available funds carries weight only after someone with purchasing authority has confirmed it.

Manufacturers often separate capital budgets from maintenance and spare-parts budgets. A freeze on one does not automatically apply to the other. Which budget a purchase belongs to is decided by finance or by the owner, not by the requesting department.

When two people at the same customer give conflicting information, the statement of the person who holds the decision right for that matter prevails: finance and the owner for money, the quality department for supplier admission, engineering for technical requirements.

When a systems integrator stands between the supplier and the machine builder, either party may place the order. Until it is settled who orders and who pays, quotations addressed to one party may never reach a person who can accept them.
Shared programmes between divisions of a large manufacturer frequently stall on the question of which division carries a component in its budget. A technical approval does not settle this question.

The stage recorded in a sales system often lags behind events. Approvals may have been completed outside the system, and an early-stage record can hide a late-stage situation. The facts of the account describe the situation better than the stage label.

Datasheet values hold under the reference conditions printed on the datasheet. Real applications differ in medium, surface, temperature, speed and load peaks. A difference between the reference condition and the application is settled by an application check based on the customer's written operating data.

Most open technical questions can be answered from documents: drawings, operating logs, medium composition, temperature profiles, tolerance limits. Customers can usually provide these electronically within days.

Some installation questions cannot be answered from documents. Clearances around moving parts, cable routes and access for maintenance are often not recorded in any drawing and are established by measuring at the machine, typically during a maintenance stop.

A requirement is a hard requirement when the customer cannot change it and the supplier cannot meet it with any product, accessory or planned development. Requirements fixed by an end customer's contract or by the final equipment design belong to this kind.

A capability gap differs from a timing problem. If no product meets a fixed requirement and none is planned, a later purchasing cycle finds the same gap. Sales effort spent on such an account is not recovered.
source: General B2B sales practice: opportunity selection

text: When a customer's documents contain two different values for the same parameter, the governing revision has to be identified before suitability can be judged. A value that may belong to another machine establishes nothing until the customer confirms which one applies.
A change to the specification during commercial discussions reopens the technical acceptance. Prices agreed for the earlier specification may not hold for the changed one.

End customers in food, pharmaceutical and hazardous-area applications pass certification requirements down to the machine builder and from there to component suppliers. A third-party certificate and a manufacturer's declaration are different documents, and one does not replace the other.
Machine builders who sell under a contract that fixes the control system cannot accept components with a different communication interface, even if the component is otherwise superior.

Customers look for a second source mainly for four reasons: unreliable deliveries, a discontinued part, a price increase, or a design change. The strength of the reason determines how much switching risk the customer will accept.

Changing a component supplier exposes the customer to the risk of machine stops. Customers limit this risk by starting with a small quantity on one machine or one line, with the incumbent part remaining in use elsewhere, and extend the change after a period of operation.

Doubt about a product and doubt about a supplier are different concerns. Doubt about a product concerns behaviour in the customer's own process: stability over a shift, in dust, through repeated starts. Doubt about a supplier concerns whether the company understands the customer's industry and will support it.
source: Adapted from SPIN Selling: distinguishing customer concerns

text: Evidence from the customer's own process answers doubt about a product. Evidence from comparable customers answers doubt about a supplier. Customers who doubt the supplier rarely make machine time or staff available for testing until that doubt is addressed.

Laboratory results confirm that a product meets its specification. Production staff give more weight to what they have seen on their own equipment, and management often follows their judgement on a change of supplier.

A supplier known in one sector is often assumed to serve only that sector. Customers from other sectors ask about service expectations, maintenance routines and operator training in their own industry before they consider the product itself.

Words such as unproven or reliability are used for both kinds of doubt. Which one is meant becomes clear from what the customer asks for next: operating evidence on its own line, or information about comparable customers.

Medium and large manufacturers admit new suppliers through a formal procedure owned by the quality department. Purchasing cannot place a first order with a supplier that has not been admitted, whatever the technical and commercial status.

Many admission procedures require an auditor to be present at the supplier's premises to see calibration handling, assembly identification and traceability. Where the procedure requires presence, certificates, photographs and video calls do not replace it.
Audit calendars of quality departments fill weeks in advance. The date of the audit often determines the date of the first order more than any commercial discussion.

Uploaded certificates usually satisfy the preliminary stage of supplier admission. The final signature may depend on further steps, and purchasing checklists are not always updated when the quality department adds one.

Machine builders calculate a component allowance for each part of a machine. A price above the allowance is rejected regardless of product quality. The buyer's target price usually reflects this allowance and has little room to move.

Volume, contract length, packaging and shipment frequency are the usual items traded against price. When the customer has already considered them and the gap remains, only a change in the unit price closes it.

A price discussion is productive once technical acceptance, supplier admission and delivery terms are complete. Price agreed while a technical question is open is often renegotiated when the question is answered.
Buyers with award authority set deadlines for price answers that follow their own approval calendar, such as a board meeting. An answer after the deadline is treated as no answer.
Design cycles of machine builders run 12 to 24 months. A component chosen for a future machine generation is ordered when detailed design begins, not when the product is first discussed.
source: Account planning practice for machine builders

text: A postponed machine programme leaves the technical approval valid. Drawings and approved supplier entries are kept and used when the programme restarts.
source: Account planning practice for machine builders

text: Exclusive supply agreements are honoured until they expire. Some oblige the customer to report competing offers to the incumbent, which is why customers under such agreements ask to receive no quotations.
source: Account planning practice for machine builders

text: When the people responsible for budget and for the programme give the same date in writing, that date describes the opportunity. Enthusiasm from staff without responsibility for either does not move it.
source: Account planning practice for machine builders

text: Notes in an account file age. A note about urgency written a quarter ago describes the situation at that time and yields to a later written statement from the responsible managers.
source: Account planning practice for machine builders

text: Export-oriented machine builders ship against contractual delivery dates with penalties for delay. A late component delays the whole machine, which is why delivery reliability often weighs more than unit price in their choice of supplier.
Builders who cannot rely on a supplier's delivery dates hold safety stock of critical components. The cost of this stock is a recurring argument for qualifying a second source.

Machines exported to the European market need CE conformity for the complete machine. The builder collects declarations for every component, and missing documents stop shipment at the end of the project.
Export customers ask for documentation in the language of the destination market and for components that are available as spare parts in that market for the service life of the machine.

Small machine builders are often run by an owner who decides on purchases personally. Larger builders separate engineering, quality, purchasing and finance, and each function holds its own decision right.
